q-315645.name: Question 1
q-315645.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{4x-1}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+{(\sqrt{4x-1}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{4x-1})^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+4x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+4x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+15.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=2$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=2$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(2)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(2)} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}-4\,(2)+15} \\  & =\sqrt{4-8+15} \\  & =\sqrt{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

S=(x−4)2+(y−2)2=(x−4)2+(4x−1+2−2)2=(x−4)2+(4x−1)2=(x−4)2+4x−1=x2−8x+16+4x−1=x2−4x+15.

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of S(x) and equate it to zero. This gives the following: S′(x)=2x−4=02x=4x=2

q-344820.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(3,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+5}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{4x+5}+2-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+4x+5 \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+4x+5 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+14.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-2 & =0 \\ 2x & =2 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=1$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $x=1.$

q-344830.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(3,-\frac{17}{2})$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-3)^{2}+{(y+\frac{17}{2})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{289}{4} \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{325}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-6x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{325}{4} \\  & ={y}^{2}+18y+\frac{325}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y+18 & =0 \\ 2y & =-18 \\ y & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=-9$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=-9.$

q-344833.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(5,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-5)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{4x}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{4x}+2-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{4x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+4x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+4x \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-6 & =0 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0,$ so $x=3$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=3$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(3)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-6(3)+25} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

q-344846.name: Question 5
q-344846.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+{(\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4})^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}+4 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0.$ Therefore, $x=1$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+6} \\  & =\sqrt{2-4+6} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
